render.title: Cytochrome c mobility and electron shuttling
render.summary: Cytochrome c is a small soluble protein in the intermembrane space. It accepts one electron from Complex III and carries it to Complex IV. Its solubility comes from its lack of transmembrane segments: it sits on the membrane surface and diffuses freely.
render.body:
Cytochrome c is a small protein that acts as an electron courier between two large protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

What it does:

At Complex III (the cytochrome bc1 complex), an electron is handed off to cytochrome c. The protein carries that single electron to Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), where it is delivered to begin the reduction of oxygen to water. Because each cytochrome c carries only one electron at a time, and Complex IV needs four electrons to reduce one oxygen molecule, four separate cytochrome c molecules must each dock and deliver before the reaction can proceed.

Why it can leave the membrane:

Most of the proteins in the electron transport chain are large, multi-subunit complexes with sections that thread back and forth through the inner membrane. These transmembrane segments anchor them firmly in place.

Cytochrome c is different. It is a relatively tiny protein (about 12,000 daltons) with no transmembrane segments at all. It sits in the intermembrane space — the narrow gap between the inner and outer mitochondrial membranes — and associates loosely with the outer surface of the inner membrane. Because it is essentially a soluble protein that only docks briefly onto Complex III or Complex IV during electron transfer, it can detach and diffuse laterally through the intermembrane space to find its next partner.

The heme group and the iron atom:

At the centre of cytochrome c is a heme group — a flat ring structure with an iron atom at its core. It is this iron atom that actually carries the electron. The iron cycles between two oxidation states: Fe3+ (oxidised, before receiving the electron) and Fe2+ (reduced, after receiving it). When cytochrome c docks onto Complex IV, the iron returns to Fe3+ by giving the electron away.

This combination — a small soluble protein with a single iron-centred heme — makes cytochrome c an efficient mobile shuttle that bridges two large membrane-bound complexes without being tied to either one.
